paragraphs: Very soon after he got his four-year-old Mitya off his hands, Fyodor Pavlovitch married a second time. This marriage lasted eight years. His second wife, Sofya Ivanovna, was also a very young girl. He took her from another province, where he had gone on some small piece of business with a Jew. Fyodor Pavlovitch was a drunkard and a vicious debauchee, but he never neglected to invest his capital. He managed his business affairs very successfully, though, no doubt, not too scrupulously. Sofya Ivanovna was the daughter of an obscure deacon, and she had been left an orphan with no relations since childhood. She grew up in the house of a general’s widow, a wealthy old lady of good position, who was both her benefactress and her tormentor. I do not know the details. I have only heard that the orphan girl, a meek and gentle creature, was once cut down from a noose she had hung from a nail in the loft. That was how terribly she suffered from the whims and endless nagging of this old woman, who was apparently not bad-hearted but had turned into an unbearable tyrant out of idleness.

Fyodor Pavlovitch made her an offer. Inquiries were made about him, and he was refused. But again, as with his first marriage, he proposed an elopement to the orphan girl. There is very little doubt that she would never have married him if she had learned a little more about him in time. But she lived in another province. Besides, what could a little girl of sixteen know about it, except that she would be better off at the bottom of the river than staying with her benefactress? So the poor child exchanged a benefactress for a benefactor. Fyodor Pavlovitch did not get a penny this time, because the general’s widow was furious. She gave them nothing and cursed them both. But he had not been counting on a dowry. What drew him was the remarkable beauty of the innocent girl, and above all her innocent look. It had a peculiar attraction for a vicious profligate who until then had admired only the coarser kinds of feminine beauty.

“Those innocent eyes slit my soul up like a razor,” he used to say afterwards, with his loathsome snigger. In a man so depraved, of course, this might mean no more than sensual attraction. He had received no dowry with his wife, and had, so to speak, taken her “from the noose,” so he did not stand on ceremony with her. He made her feel that she had “wronged” him. He took advantage of her extraordinary meekness and submissiveness to trample on the most elementary decencies of marriage. He gathered loose women into his house and held drunken orgies in his wife’s presence. To show how bad things had become, I may mention that Grigory took the new mistress’s side. He was the gloomy, stupid, obstinate, argumentative servant who had always hated his first mistress, Adelaïda Ivanovna. He championed her cause, abusing Fyodor Pavlovitch in a way that hardly suited a servant, and on one occasion he broke up the revels and drove all the disorderly women out of the house. In the end this unhappy young woman, who had been kept in terror since childhood, fell into the kind of nervous disease most often found in peasant women, who are said to be “possessed by devils.” At times, after terrible fits of hysterics, she even lost her reason. Yet she bore Fyodor Pavlovitch two sons, Ivan and Alexey. The elder was born in the first year of the marriage and the second three years later. When she died, little Alexey was in his fourth year. Strange as it seems, I know that he remembered his mother all his life, like a dream, of course. At her death almost exactly the same thing happened to the two little boys as had happened to their elder brother, Mitya. Their father completely forgot and abandoned them. They were looked after by the same Grigory and lived in his cottage, and that is where the tyrannical old lady who had brought up their mother found them. She was still alive, and in all those eight years she had not forgotten the insult done to her. All that time she had been getting exact information about how her Sofya lived. When she heard of her illness and her hideous surroundings, she declared aloud to her retainers, two or three times:
“It serves her right. God has punished her for her ingratitude.”

Exactly three months after Sofya Ivanovna’s death, the general’s widow suddenly appeared in our town and went straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. She spent only half an hour in the town, but she did a great deal in it. It was evening. Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom she had not seen for those eight years, came in to her drunk. The story is that the instant she saw him, without any kind of explanation, she gave him two good, resounding slaps in the face, seized him by a tuft of hair, and shook him three times up and down. Then, without a word, she went straight to the cottage where the two boys were. She saw at the first glance that they were unwashed and in dirty linen, and she promptly gave Grigory a box on the ear too. She announced that she would carry off both children, wrapped them just as they were in a rug, put them in the carriage, and drove off to her own town. Grigory took the blow like a devoted slave, without a word. When he escorted the old lady to her carriage, he made her a low bow and declared solemnly that “God would repay her for the orphans.” “You are a blockhead all the same,” the old lady shouted to him as she drove away.

Fyodor Pavlovitch thought it over and decided that this was a good thing. He gave the general’s widow his formal consent to any proposal about his children’s education. As for the slaps she had given him, he drove all over the town telling the story.

It happened that the old lady died soon after this, but in her will she left the boys a thousand roubles each “for their instruction, and so that all be spent on them exclusively, with the condition that it be so portioned out as to last till they are twenty-one, for it is more than adequate provision for such children. If other people think fit to throw away their money, let them.” I have not read the will myself, but I heard there was something queer of the sort, very whimsically expressed. The principal heir was Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the Marshal of Nobility of the province, and he turned out to be an honest man. He wrote to Fyodor Pavlovitch and saw at once that he could get nothing out of him for his children’s education. (Fyodor Pavlovitch never flatly refused, but only put things off, as he always did in such cases, and was, in fact, at times effusively sentimental.) So Yefim Petrovitch took a personal interest in the orphans. He became especially fond of the younger, Alexey, who lived for a long while as one of his family. I ask the reader to note this from the beginning. And it was to Yefim Petrovitch, a man of a generosity and humanity rarely met with, that the young people owed their education and upbringing more than to anyone. He kept the two thousand roubles the general’s widow had left them intact, so that by the time they came of age, interest had doubled their portions. He educated them both at his own expense, and he certainly spent far more than a thousand roubles on each of them. I won’t go into a detailed account of their boyhood and youth. I will only mention a few of the most important events. Of the elder, Ivan, I will only say that he grew into a rather morose and reserved boy, though far from timid. By the age of ten he had realized that they were living not in their own home but on other people’s charity, and that their father was a man it was disgraceful to speak of. This boy began very early, almost in his infancy (so they say, at least), to show a brilliant and unusual gift for learning. I don’t know exactly why, but he left Yefim Petrovitch’s family when he was barely thirteen. He entered a Moscow gymnasium and boarded with an experienced and celebrated teacher, an old friend of Yefim Petrovitch. Ivan used to say afterwards that all this was due to the “ardor for good works” of Yefim Petrovitch, who was taken with the idea that a boy of genius should be trained by a teacher of genius. But neither Yefim Petrovitch nor this teacher was still alive when the young man finished at the gymnasium and entered the university. Yefim Petrovitch had made no arrangement for paying out the tyrannical old lady’s legacy, which had grown from one thousand to two. It was delayed by the formalities that are unavoidable in Russia, and the young man was in great straits for his first two years at the university, since he had to keep himself the whole time he was studying. It must be noted that he did not even try to get in touch with his father. Perhaps it was pride, or contempt for him. Perhaps it was his cool common sense, which told him that he would get no real help from such a father. However that may be, the young man was not at all despondent, and he managed to find work. At first he gave lessons at sixpence a time, and afterwards he got paragraphs on street incidents into the newspapers under the signature of “Eye-Witness.” These paragraphs, it was said, were so interesting and piquant that they were soon taken. This alone showed the young man’s practical and intellectual superiority over the masses of needy and unfortunate students of both sexes, who hang about the offices of the newspapers and journals, unable to think of anything better than endless pleas for copying and translations from the French. Once he had got in touch with the editors, Ivan Fyodorovitch always kept up his connection with them. In his last years at the university he published brilliant reviews of books on various special subjects, so that he became well known in literary circles. But only in his final year did he suddenly attract the attention of a far wider circle of readers, so that a great many people noticed and remembered him. It was a rather curious incident. He had just left the university and was preparing to go abroad on his two thousand roubles. Ivan Fyodorovitch published in one of the more important journals a strange article, which drew general notice. Its subject was one he might have been supposed to know nothing about, since he was a student of natural science. The article dealt with a question that was being debated everywhere at the time, the position of the ecclesiastical courts. After discussing several opinions on the matter, he went on to explain his own view. What was most striking about the article was its tone and its unexpected conclusion. Many of the Church party took him without question as being on their side. And yet not only the secularists but even atheists joined them in applauding it. Finally some shrewd people suggested that the article was nothing but an impudent satirical burlesque. I mention this incident particularly because the article found its way into the famous monastery in our neighborhood. The monks there were especially interested in the question of the ecclesiastical courts, and they were completely bewildered by it. When they learned the author’s name, they were interested to find that he was a native of the town and the son of “that Fyodor Pavlovitch.” And just then the author himself appeared among us.

Why Ivan Fyodorovitch had come among us, I remember asking myself at the time with a certain uneasiness. This fateful visit was the first step toward so many consequences, and I never fully explained it to myself. On the face of it, it seemed strange that a young man so learned, so proud, and apparently so cautious should suddenly visit such an infamous house, and a father who had ignored him all his life. His father hardly knew him, never thought of him, and would not under any circumstances have given him money, though he was always afraid that his sons Ivan and Alexey would come and ask him for it. And here was the young man staying in the house of such a father. He had been living with him for two months, and they were on the best possible terms. This last fact astonished many others as well as me. Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, of whom we have spoken already, the cousin of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s first wife, happened to be in the neighborhood again, on a visit to his estate. He had come from Paris, which was his permanent home. I remember that he was more surprised than anyone when he met the young man. Ivan interested him extremely. He sometimes argued with him, and not without an inner pang compared his own learning with Ivan’s.

“He is proud,” he used to say, “he will never be short of pennies. He has money enough to go abroad now. What does he want here? Anyone can see he hasn’t come for money, because his father would never give him any. He has no taste for drink and dissipation, and yet his father can’t do without him. They get on so well together!”

That was the truth. The young man had an unmistakable influence over his father. Fyodor Pavlovitch positively seemed to be behaving more decently, and at times even seemed ready to obey his son, though he was often extremely and even spitefully perverse.

It was only later that we learned that Ivan had come partly at the request, and in the interests, of his elder brother Dmitri. He saw Dmitri for the first time on this very visit, though before leaving Moscow he had been writing to him about an important matter that concerned Dmitri more than himself. The reader will learn fully in due time what that business was. Yet even when I did know about this special circumstance, I still felt Ivan Fyodorovitch to be an enigmatic figure, and I thought his visit rather mysterious.

I may add that Ivan appeared at the time in the light of a mediator between his father and his elder brother Dmitri, who was in open quarrel with his father and was even planning to bring a lawsuit against him.

The family, I repeat, was now united for the first time, and some of its members met for the first time in their lives. The younger brother, Alexey, had already been a year among us, having been the first of the three to arrive. It is of this brother Alexey that I find it hardest to speak in this introduction. Yet I must give some preliminary account of him, if only to explain one queer fact: I have to introduce my hero to the reader wearing the cassock of a novice. Yes, he had been in our monastery for the last year, and seemed willing to be shut up there for the rest of his life.
